questions.title: First-part subclavian branch identification
questions.question: This structure is a branch from…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The costocervical trunk is a branch of the subclavian artery's SECOND part (behind scalenus anterior), not the vessel this image points at.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The arch of the aorta gives the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, not this vessel.
explanations.C: Correct. The first part of the subclavian artery, medial to scalenus anterior, gives three branches — the vertebral artery, the internal thoracic artery and the thyrocervical trunk. This image points to a structure originating from this first part. Recognising the first part as the branch-bearing segment (rather than the second, which gives only the costocervical trunk, or the third, which usually gives none) is the key discrimination this item tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thyrocervical trunk is itself one of the branches OF the first part of the subclavian artery, not the parent vessel the image is pointing to.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the first part of the subclavian artery as the branch-bearing segment proximal to scalenus anterior.

questions.title: Neck vessel identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Correct. The subclavian artery arches over the cervical pleura and first rib on its way to become the axillary artery, a course and position distinct from the common carotid artery's straight ascent in the carotid sheath. This identification depends on the vessel's characteristic arching course at the root of the neck.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The common carotid artery ascends within the carotid sheath alongside the internal jugular vein, without an arching course over the first rib, and gives no branch in the neck.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery is a first-part subclavian branch that descends into the thorax behind the costal cartilages, not a vessel arching at the root of the neck.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The suprascapular artery is a thyrocervical-trunk branch crossing the posterior triangle toward the scapula, a smaller and more posterior vessel than the one this image points to.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the subclavian artery from the common carotid, internal thoracic and suprascapular arteries by course and position.

questions.title: Posterior cricoarytenoid action
questions.question: Action of this muscle is…

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adduction (closing the rima glottidis) is performed by the lateral cricoarytenoid and the arytenoid muscles, not by the muscle pictured here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Closing the laryngeal inlet is a sphincteric action of the aryepiglottic and oblique arytenoid fibres during swallowing, a different action from the one this muscle performs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stretching (tensing) the vocal cords is the cricothyroid's action, the one intrinsic muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve rather than the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanations.D: Correct. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the ONLY abductor of the vocal folds — it rotates the arytenoid cartilage to swing the vocal process laterally, opening the airway. Its unique abductor role is why bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (paralysing this muscle on both sides) is a life-threatening airway emergency, since nothing else can open the rima glottidis. This muscle's isolated action is one of the highest-yield facts in laryngeal anatomy.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds.

questions.title: Laryngeal cartilage identification (recovered)
questions.question: This structure refers to… (laryngeal cartilage/fold identification, recovered at 200 dpi render, previously flagged unreadable)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The thyroid cartilage is the largest laryngeal cartilage, forming the laryngeal prominence anteriorly, and is not the structure this pointer identifies.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cricoid cartilage is the single complete cartilaginous ring of the airway, sitting below the thyroid cartilage, distinct from the paired structure pointed to here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The epiglottis is the leaf-shaped elastic cartilage attached to the back of the thyroid cartilage, bounding the laryngeal inlet anteriorly — a different, unpaired structure from the one identified.
explanations.D: Correct. The arytenoid cartilages are paired, pyramidal cartilages sitting on the cricoid lamina posteriorly, and each gives attachment to a vocal fold via its vocal process. This item, recovered on a 200 dpi render after the page's text-extraction was initially flagged unreadable, confirms this pyramidal cartilage as the correctly pointed structure.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the arytenoid cartilage among the laryngeal cartilages.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (page recovered; Step-1 triage had flagged it text-extraction-unreadable)

questions.title: Laryngeal inlet boundary identification
questions.question: Red arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiglottis is the leaf-shaped cartilage bounding the laryngeal inlet anteriorly, a separate structure from the fold pointed to on each side of the inlet.
explanations.B: Correct. The aryepiglottic fold runs from the epiglottis to the arytenoid cartilage on each side, bounding the laryngeal inlet laterally. It is a fold of mucosa over an underlying muscle, distinct from the vestibular and vocal folds that divide the laryngeal cavity itself lower down.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The false vocal cord (vestibular fold) is an internal cavity divider between the vestibule and the ventricle, at a level below the laryngeal inlet, not one of its side boundaries.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cricoid cartilage is the complete ring below the vocal folds, an entirely different structure at a lower level than the laryngeal inlet.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the aryepiglottic fold as a lateral boundary of the laryngeal inlet.

questions.title: Costotransverse joint identification
questions.question: This part articulates with…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The costotransverse ligament stabilises the joint but is a ligament, not the bony structure the rib's tubercle actually articulates with.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The demifacet is at the rib's HEAD, forming the costovertebral joint with the vertebral body/disc, a different joint from the one the pointed part forms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The costal cartilage connects the rib's anterior (sternal) end to the sternum, an entirely different articulation from the one pictured here.
explanations.D: Correct. The rib's tubercle articulates with the transverse process of the numerically corresponding vertebra, forming the costotransverse joint — the second of the two synovial joints a typical rib makes with the vertebral column (the other being the costovertebral joint at the rib's head). This joint is stabilised by the costotransverse ligaments.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Identify the transverse process as the vertebral partner of the rib tubercle at the costotransverse joint.

questions.title: First-rib neurovascular relation identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stellate ganglion lies at the neck of the first rib, close to this structure but is a sympathetic chain ganglion, not the somatic nerve trunk this image points to.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Sympathetic ganglion" is too generic and, like option A, names the autonomic structure in this region rather than the somatic brachial-plexus trunk being identified.
explanations.C: Correct. The lower trunk of the brachial plexus crosses the first rib in the same groove as the subclavian artery, posterior to the scalene tubercle, closely related to (but distinct from) the stellate ganglion at the rib's neck. Recognising which structure in this crowded region is the somatic nerve trunk versus the sympathetic ganglion is the discrimination this item tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ventral rami contribute to the roots of the brachial plexus more proximally, in the interscalene region, rather than at the level of the first rib pictured here.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the brachial plexus's lower trunk from the stellate ganglion at the neck of the first rib.

questions.title: Subclavian-axillary continuity
questions.question: Subclavian artery continuity with the axillary artery (D-axillary artery legible; full stem context recovered as a borderline upper-limb/thorax framing item, per the triage)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachial artery is the NEXT continuation, beyond the axillary artery, beginning at the lower border of teres major — one continuity step further than what is being asked here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The suprascapular artery is a thyrocervical-trunk branch supplying the scapular region, not the named continuation of the subclavian artery itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thoracoacromial artery is a branch OF the axillary artery, not the vessel the subclavian artery is renamed as.
explanations.D: Correct. The subclavian artery's third part, lateral to scalenus anterior, continues at the outer border of the first rib as the axillary artery. This is the standard anatomical landmark marking the name change, and the third part itself gives no named branch before the continuation. The corresponding change back to the brachial artery happens further down the limb, at the lower border of teres major.

questions.learning_objective: State that the subclavian artery is renamed the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; stem partly under-legible per the Step-1 triage, option D confirmed

questions.title: Brachiocephalic vein formation (printed key discrepancy)
questions.question: This structure is formed from…

options.A: Left external jugular + left subclavian vein
options.B: Left internal + left external jugular vein
options.D: Right subclavian + right internal jugular vein

explanations.A: Incorrect. The left external jugular vein is not the pairing partner in the standard brachiocephalic-vein union; the standard union is an internal jugular plus a subclavian vein on the same side.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two jugular veins (internal + external) of the same side do not unite to form a brachiocephalic vein; the union is always one internal jugular plus one subclavian vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior vena cava forms further downstream, from the union of the TWO brachiocephalic veins behind the first right costal cartilage — a separate, later union from the one this item asks about.
explanations.D: Correct, as printed — the bank's own ink-marked key selects this pairing. As printed this describes the formation of the RIGHT brachiocephalic vein (right subclavian + right internal jugular vein), the standard union for that side. Recorded here exactly as the source keys it; a genuine ambiguity remains about which side's brachiocephalic vein the underlying (unseen) image actually shows, since the department's own teaching (see article ART-CVS-AU106-NECK-VESSELS-VEINS-HEART-SURFACE) states the identical rule applies symmetrically to the left vein as well, from left internal jugular + left subclavian vein.

questions.subtopic: Great Veins of the Neck and Thorax
questions.learning_objective: State that each brachiocephalic vein forms from that side's internal jugular plus subclavian vein.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; printed key records the right-sided union, see CON-CVS-34440D1CAD13C0 Conflicts/Uncertainty for the left/right identity discussion

questions.title: Thyrocervical trunk branch identification
questions.question: Which… branch from a pointed vessel

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior cerebral artery is an intracranial branch of the internal carotid artery, unrelated to the extracranial vessel this item points to.
explanations.B: Correct. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery, grooving the submandibular gland before crossing the mandible at the anterior border of masseter and running a tortuous course toward the medial angle of the eye. This distinguishes it from the thyrocervical trunk's own branches (inferior thyroid, transverse cervical, suprascapular), which arise from the subclavian system rather than the carotid system.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (subclavian territory), not from the vessel this item points to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The subclavian artery is the PARENT vessel of the thyrocervical trunk, not a branch arising from a smaller vessel in this region.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish carotid-system branches (e.g. facial artery) from subclavian/thyrocervical-system branches.

questions.title: Nasal bone identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The frontal bone forms the upper forehead and part of the orbit above the nasal bones, articulating with them but not being the pointed structure itself.
explanations.B: Correct. The paired nasal bones articulate with the frontal bone above and the frontal processes of the maxilla on each side. Together they form the bony bridge of the nose and the upper part of the piriform aperture's boundary. The greater part of the nasal cavity's roof, further back, is formed instead by the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, not by these bones.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sphenoid bone lies deep and posterior, contributing to the roof of the nasal cavity near the sphenoethmoidal recess, not to the external bridge of the nose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nasal septum is a midline structure dividing the cavity into two halves, not the paired external bony bridge this arrow points to.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the nasal bones as forming the bridge of the nose.

questions.title: Paranasal sinus drainage identification
questions.question: Which… opens in this area

explanations.A: Incorrect. The posterior ethmoidal air cells open into the SUPERIOR meatus, a different location from the area this item points to.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary sinus opens into the middle meatus via the hiatus semilunaris, a specific groove-based route distinct from the ethmoidal bulla area this item identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sphenoidal sinus bypasses the meatal system entirely, opening into the sphenoethmoidal recess above and behind the superior concha — a different location again.
explanations.D: Correct. The middle ethmoidal air cells open onto or near the ethmoidal bulla, a rounded bulge in the middle meatus above the hiatus semilunaris. This is the specific landmark this item's pointer identifies. It is distinct from the anterior ethmoidal cells' and the frontal/maxillary sinuses' shared hiatus-semilunaris drainage route.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Locate the middle ethmoidal air cells' drainage onto the ethmoidal bulla, distinct from the hiatus semilunaris route.

questions.title: External carotid branch identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Laryngeal artery" is not a standard named branch at this level; the superior laryngeal artery is a branch of the superior thyroid artery, at a different point on the external carotid tree.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lingual artery is a separate external carotid branch supplying the tongue, arising and coursing differently from the vessel this arrow points to.
explanations.C: Correct. The facial artery is one of the eight named branches of the external carotid artery, grooving the submandibular gland and following a tortuous course toward the medial angle of the eye. This course and position distinguishes it from the lingual, laryngeal (via superior thyroid) and ophthalmic vessels. Recognising the facial artery by its characteristic path, rather than by name alone, is the skill this item tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the INTERNAL carotid artery (via the cranial cavity), not of the external carotid tree this image points into.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the facial artery among the external carotid artery's branches.

questions.title: Facial artery termination
questions.question: Termination of this vessel at…

explanations.A: Incorrect. The neck of the mandible is where the maxillary artery, a different external carotid terminal branch, begins its deep course — not where the vessel in this item ends.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The base of the skull is where the internal carotid artery enters the cranial cavity, not where an external carotid branch terminates in the neck.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The C4/5 disc level is where the common carotid artery typically bifurcates, not the termination point being asked about here.
explanations.D: Correct. The vessel terminates near the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, at the level where the common carotid artery bifurcates into internal and external carotid arteries. This is consistent with the facial artery's origin from the external carotid at this level, before its own tortuous course toward the face. Identifying this shared termination/origin level ties the facial artery's course back to the carotid bifurcation.

questions.learning_objective: Relate the level of the carotid bifurcation (upper border of thyroid cartilage) to the origin of the external carotid's branches.

questions.title: Nasal septum/vestibule identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to… (sagittal section of nose)

explanations.A: Incorrect. The vomer is the postero-inferior bony part of the septum, a different, more posterior structure from the one this arrow points to.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The septal cartilage is the antero-inferior part of the septum, filling the gap between the ethmoid's perpendicular plate and the vomer, not the region this item identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ethmoidal bulla is a lateral-wall landmark for middle-meatus drainage, not a septal or anterior-cavity structure like the one pictured here.
explanations.D: Correct. The vestibule is the small, hair-bearing anterior part of the nasal cavity just inside the nostril, lined by skin rather than respiratory mucosa. It is anatomically and histologically distinct from the deeper septal and lateral-wall structures, which are lined by ciliated respiratory epithelium. This lining difference is the reason the vestibule alone grows hair, unlike the rest of the nasal cavity.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the nasal vestibule as the skin-lined anterior part of the nasal cavity.

questions.title: Middle meatus drainage identification
questions.question: Which… structure opens in this area

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal air cells open into the middle meatus via the hiatus semilunaris, a different specific route from the one this item points to.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sphenoidal sinus opens into the sphenoethmoidal recess, well above and behind this area, not into the inferior meatus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The maxillary sinus also drains into the middle meatus (not the area pictured here), via the hiatus semilunaris rather than this opening.
explanations.D: Correct. The nasolacrimal duct opens into the INFERIOR meatus, carrying tears from the lacrimal sac down into the nasal cavity. It is the one drainage route in this region that is not a paranasal sinus and is not routed through the middle meatus like the ethmoidal and maxillary sinuses. This is why a blocked nasolacrimal duct produces watering of the eye rather than nasal congestion.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the nasolacrimal duct's inferior-meatus opening from the paranasal sinuses' middle/superior-meatus and sphenoethmoidal-recess drainage.

questions.title: Inferior vena cava origin (recovered, shares page with Q46)
questions.question: This structure starts at… (second, previously uncatalogued question sharing page 46's image)

explanations.A: Correct. The inferior vena cava forms at the level of L5, behind and to the right of the aortic bifurcation, by the union of the two common iliac veins. This recovered item independently corroborates the same fact recorded on CON-CVS-37D544FD59E6D3, whose only other source (the Telegram addendum bank) carries a genuine printed-key inconsistency mixing up the IVC with a brachiocephalic vein — this ink-bank item is unaffected by that error and confirms the correct level directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. L3 is not the level of the aortic bifurcation or the common iliac veins' union; it is too high.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T12 is the level of the diaphragm's aortic opening, an entirely different, much higher landmark from the IVC's formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S1 is below the actual level of the IVC's formation (L5), too low to be correct.

questions.subtopic: Great Veins of the Neck and Thorax
questions.learning_objective: State that the inferior vena cava forms at L5 from the union of the two common iliac veins.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi (recovered, page 46, second question sharing the page's image)

questions.title: First-rib muscle attachment identification
questions.question: This arrow gives attachment for…

explanations.A: Incorrect. Serratus anterior's first digitation attaches to the first rib's shaft more anteriorly, a different point from the one this arrow marks.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Scalenus anterior inserts at the scalene tubercle, on the first rib's upper surface, which is the landmark separating the vein groove from the artery/nerve groove — not the point this arrow indicates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subclavius attaches to the first costal cartilage more anteriorly and inferiorly, not the point marked here.
explanations.D: Correct. Scalenus medius attaches posterior to the groove for the subclavian artery and the brachial plexus's lower trunk, on the first rib's upper surface. This is the posterior-most of the muscle attachments on this rib, distinguishing it from scalenus anterior's more anterior insertion at the scalene tubercle. The two scalene attachments therefore bracket the artery/nerve groove between them.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish scalenus medius's posterior first-rib attachment from scalenus anterior's attachment at the scalene tubercle.

questions.title: Thoracic vertebra part identification (red arrow)
questions.question: This red arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Correct. The pedicle is a short, thick projection connecting the vertebral body to the lamina, notched above and below to help form the intervertebral foramina. This is the structure the red arrow points to on this typical thoracic vertebra. The neighbouring green arrow, on the same image, marks a second example of the same structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lamina completes the vertebral arch posterior to the pedicle, meeting its counterpart in the midline; this is the structure the GREEN arrow on the same image points to instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spinous process is the long, downward-sloping projection at the back of the vertebral arch, a different part from the one the red arrow marks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The transverse process projects laterally at the pedicle-lamina junction and carries the costal facet for the rib tubercle, a different projection from the one identified here.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Identify the pedicle among the parts of a typical thoracic vertebra.

questions.title: Thoracic vertebra part identification (green arrow)
questions.question: This green arrow refers to… (same image and option set as the red-arrow item on this page)

explanations.A: Correct, as printed. The confirmed key for the green arrow, like the red arrow, selects the pedicle per the bank's own ink-marked key table. Recorded exactly as keyed; the two pointers on this image mark two comparable examples of the same structure class (pedicle) at different points, a plausible teaching device for reinforcing pedicle recognition rather than an error.
explanations.B: Incorrect per the printed key. The lamina completes the vertebral arch posterior to the pedicle; if this were the tested structure it would need its own distinguishing description separate from the red arrow's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spinous process is the long downward-sloping projection, a visually distinct part from the pedicle this item's key selects.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The transverse process carries the costal facet for the rib tubercle, a laterally projecting part distinct from the pedicle identified by the key.

questions.subject: msk
questions.learning_objective: Identify the pedicle among the parts of a typical thoracic vertebra, reinforced by a second labelled point on the same image.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; both red- and green-arrow items on p.48 key to pedicle as printed

questions.title: Neck vessel identification (corrected key)
questions.question: Options only: inferior thyroid a. / external carotid a. / superior thyroid a. / vertebral a. (full stem not recovered; ink-key confirmed at 200 dpi corrects the Step-1 guess)

explanations.A: Incorrect per the confirmed key. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, a plausible-sounding distractor in this neck-vessel identification set but not the confirmed answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external carotid artery is a much larger, more anterior vessel than the one this item's confirmed key identifies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery, again not the confirmed answer for this item.
explanations.D: Correct, as confirmed at 200 dpi render. This is the vertebral artery, a first-part branch of the subclavian artery, ascending through the transverse foramina of the upper six cervical vertebrae toward the brain. The render pass corrects the Step-1 triage's provisional guess, which — working only from the single legible option "D" — could not confirm the identity as a thyrocervical-trunk or external-carotid branch instead.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the vertebral artery among the named vessels of the neck.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; corrects the Step-1 triage's provisional under-confident reading, see coverage/AU-MED-106-anatomy-triage.md

questions.title: Laryngeal sensory nerve supply (corrected, full stem recovered)
questions.question: This structure is supplied by which sensory nerve

explanations.A: Incorrect per the confirmed key. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is chiefly MOTOR to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid), with sensory supply only below the vocal folds — not the answer this fully-legible stem confirms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external laryngeal nerve is motor to cricothyroid alone, not a sensory nerve to the region this item asks about.
explanations.C: Correct, as confirmed once the full stem became legible at 200 dpi. The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, is purely sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds (down to and including their upper surface). This corrects the Step-1 triage, which had recorded only option A (recurrent laryngeal nerve) as legible and so could not classify the item with confidence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Vagus nerve trunk" is too generic; the specific sensory branch supplying this region is the internal laryngeal nerve, not the parent vagus trunk itself.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the internal laryngeal nerve as the sensory supply above the vocal folds, distinct from the motor recurrent and external laryngeal nerves.

field_notes.keySource: ink-annotated key confirmed 200 dpi; full stem recovered, corrects the Step-1 triage's under-legible reading (only option A visible then)

questions.title: Paranasal sinus drainage identification (2nd instance)
questions.question: This structure opens in…

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Maxillary bone" names a bone, not a drainage route; the maxillary sinus (housed in this bone) drains through the hiatus semilunaris, the structure this item actually asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The frontal sinus, housed in the frontal bone, also drains via the hiatus semilunaris — again naming the wrong kind of structure (a bone rather than the drainage groove itself).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ethmoidal bulla is where the MIDDLE ethmoidal cells drain, a bulge above the hiatus rather than the groove this item identifies.
explanations.D: Correct. The hiatus semilunaris is the curved groove on the lateral nasal wall, under the middle concha, that the frontal sinus, the maxillary sinus and the anterior ethmoidal cells all drain through into the middle meatus. This single groove therefore serves three separate drainage sources at once. Recognising it as a shared route, rather than assigning it to only one sinus, is the point of this item.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the hiatus semilunaris as the shared drainage groove for the frontal sinus, maxillary sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells.

questions.title: Laryngeal cavity subdivision identification
questions.question: This arrow refers to…

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Sinus of larynx" and the ventricle are related but the pointer identifies the saccule specifically — its small anterior recess, not the ventricle as a whole.
explanations.B: Correct. The saccule of the larynx is a small anterior recess of the laryngeal ventricle, the space between the vestibular and vocal folds on each side. It extends upward and is distinguishable from the vestibule (the space above the false folds) and from the ventricle proper. Confusing these three closely related spaces is a common source of error in laryngeal cavity questions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The true vocal cords (vocal folds) are the lower pair of folds bounding the rima glottidis, a different structure from the small recess this arrow points to.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vestibule is the whole space above the vestibular (false) folds, a larger region than the specific small recess (the saccule) this item identifies.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the laryngeal saccule as the small anterior recess of the laryngeal ventricle.
